items.name: Salt March
clues: A colonial monopoly and tax on something that every household needed to cook.
A lawyer turned independence leader set off with 78 followers. Thousands more joined along the way.
They walked about 390 kilometres in 24 days to the sea, and then made exactly what the law said they couldn’t.
March and April 1930, from Ahmedabad to the coast at Dandi, in India.
More than 60,000 people were arrested in the campaign that followed, including its leader.
Gandhi’s march, named after the stuff you shake onto your chips.

items.name: Monday demonstrations
clues: The freedom to travel, free elections and the end of a one-party state.
It started with a few people leaving a weekly prayer for peace in a city-centre church.
Every week, crowds walked round the city’s ring road carrying candles and chanting “We are the people”.
Autumn 1989, Leipzig, East Germany. On 9 October, about 70,000 people took part, and the security forces held back.
A month later, the Berlin Wall opened.
Named after the day of the week they were held on: in German, the Montagsdemonstrationen.

items.name: Boston Tea Party
clues: A tax imposed by a parliament in which the people paying it had no say.
Colonists, some of them in disguise, organised by a group called the Sons of Liberty.
At night, they boarded three ships and threw 342 chests of cargo into the water.
December 1773, in a harbour in Massachusetts.
Britain closed the port as a punishment. Less than two years later, the War of Independence began.
Named after the city, and a very British drink.

items.name: Occupy Wall Street
clues: Inequality, and the banks that had been rescued with public money after the financial crisis.
Students, activists and unemployed people who said they spoke for “the 99%”.
Instead of marching, they camped: tents, a kitchen, a library, and a “human microphone” that repeated speeches without loudspeakers.
It began on 17 September 2011 in a small park in New York’s financial district.
Similar camps spread to hundreds of cities, including one outside the European Central Bank in Frankfurt.
Its name tells you to take over the New York street where the big banks are.

items.name: Montgomery bus boycott
clues: Rules on city buses that forced Black passengers to give up their seats to white passengers.
Almost the whole Black community of one city, led by a 26-year-old pastor who later became world-famous.
For more than a year, they walked or shared cars, often in car pools organised by churches, rather than ride.
December 1955 to December 1956, Alabama.
The US Supreme Court upheld a ruling that segregated seating on the buses was unconstitutional.
It started when Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat, and it’s named after Alabama’s capital.

items.name: March on Washington
aliases: March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom
clues: Jobs and freedom, said its official name, for people who were still treated as second-class citizens.
About 250,000 people, Black and white, plus singers such as Bob Dylan and Joan Baez.
They gathered at the memorial to a president and filled the space around a long reflecting pool.
28 August 1963, in the US capital.
The Civil Rights Act followed in 1964, and the Voting Rights Act in 1965.
Famous for Dr King’s “I have a dream” speech, and named after the city where it happened.
